newsitem.title: USA: Warm welcome, uphill climb for U.N. chief in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Warm welcome, uphill climb for U.N. chief in U.S.

text.p: American political leaders have welcomed the new United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan warmly in his uphill battle to get Washington to pay its huge debt that is crippling the world body.
Everyone wanted to see him as he undertook an intense three-day schedule of meetings that began on Wednesday in what will likely be among his most important visits of his five-year term.

He meets U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday and the traditional foe of the United Nations, Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms (R-N.C.). His schedule includes Congressional leaders Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.) and Trent Lott (R-Miss) and a host of other legislators and committee heads.

On one hand, Republican leaders have expressed a desire to pay off the more than $1 billion the United States owes the United Nations. On the other, unilateral conditions attached to the funds appear to increase far beyond the power of any U.N. chief to deliver.

Representative Benjamin Gilman (R-N.Y.), chairman of the House International Relations Committee, said U.S. dues should be lowered from 25 to 20 percent of the U.N. regular budget, which is calculated by the wealth of a country that puts the United States at 27 percent.
According to those at the meeting, Gilman also said U.N. salaries could not be raised and the world body would have to issue a "code of conduct" which he did not spell out.

While legally the United States owes the world body $1.3 billion, the computation in Washington is $500 million less because of unilateral deductions by Congress over the years, especially since Republicans came to power in 1994.
Annan, a 58-year old Ghanaian, who took office in January with the help of the Clinton administration, is already working on reform plans that have to be approved by U.N. member states.
But unlike his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, he intends to draw up a blueprint by mid-year rather than leave it to 185 states to take the initiative.
Annan dwelled on several themes in Washington among them that a country "can't be a delinquent and a good leader," and that "a good leader sometimes has to be a good follower."
"War is a failure of diplomacy. If that is indeed correct, than surely diplomacy is a first line of defence," he said.
At a reception for over 100 people, Vice President Al Gore was reported to have told the secretary-general the administration was committed to fighting for the U.N. funds.
"We will do our part. We respect you for the person you are and the leader you have become. We will pay," he said. "You are among friends," adding that friends sometimes disagree.
Annan replied, that "the world has changed and we must change." He said the United States should not only use the United Nations to further its national interests but it "should also lead."
"We must reform," he added. "I will do my part but we are in it together. We either hang together or hang separately."
And in a mischievous note, Annan referred to accusations from radical militia who insist the United Nations is trying to take over the world and its members fly around America in black helicopters.
"Tell them that we have no black helicopters. We have no designs on the United States. We could not even tame Somalia."
